items.q: Which test fits the firm's question of whether age group and main news source are related?
options: A two-sample z test for <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_1 - p_2</annotation></semantics></math>
A chi-square test for independence
A one-proportion z test for the share who use TV

items.q: Which hypotheses fit this test?
options: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math>: there is an association; <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_a</annotation></semantics></math>: there is no association

<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math>: older adults in the city prefer TV news; <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_a</annotation></semantics></math>: older adults in the city do not prefer TV news

<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math>: age group and news source are not associated among the city's adults; <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_a</annotation></semantics></math>: they are associated

<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math>: the proportions of adults in the three age groups are equal; <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_a</annotation></semantics></math>: they are not

items.q: If <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math> is true, what is the expected count of adults aged 55 and older whose main source is TV?

mistakes.why: That is the observed count. The expected count is what <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math> predicts: row total times column total over the grand total.
That splits 400 equally over the nine cells. Expected counts follow the row and column totals.

That splits the 55 and older row equally over the three sources. Under <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math> the row follows the overall column pattern.

items.q: Write the expression for the expected count of adults aged 18 to 34 whose main source is news websites, then give its value.

mistakes.why: That uses the social media or TV column total, 130. The news websites column total is 140.
Multiply the row and column totals, then divide by the grand total.

items.q: Which statement correctly checks the large counts condition for this chi-square test?
options: The sample of 400 is at least 30
The smallest expected count is 39, so every expected count is at least 5
The expected counts add up to 400, the sample size
The smallest observed count is 18, so the observed counts are at least 10

items.q: Which test fits the district's question of whether the travel mode distributions differ among the schools?
options: A chi-square test for homogeneity
A chi-square test for independence
Three one-proportion z tests
A two-sample z test for the bus proportions

items.q: Which null hypothesis fits this test?
options: The three schools have the same number of students
The distribution of travel mode is different at each school
Bus, car and walking are equally common at each of the schools
The travel mode distribution is the same at all three schools

items.q: If <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math> is true, what is the expected count of East students who walk or bike?

mistakes.why: That is the observed count. Use row total times column total over the grand total.
That splits the walkers equally among the schools, but the schools have different sample sizes.

items.q: Which statement checks the 10% condition for this test?
options: Each expected count is at least 10% of its row total
At least 10% of each sample walks or bikes
Each sample is less than 10% of the students at its own school
The 400 students are less than 10% of the district's adults

items.q: Which of these changes to the table would make the chi-square statistic larger, with the totals kept the same?
options: Expected counts that equal the observed counts
Observed counts that sit closer to their expected counts
Listing the schools in a different order
Observed counts farther from their expected counts

items.q: Why is an expected count equal to (row total)(column total) divided by the grand total?
options: It spreads the grand total equally over the cells of the table
It is the average of the row total and the column total
It makes the expected counts as close as possible to the observed counts in the table
With no association, each row shares the whole table's column proportions

items.q: A vet randomly assigns 150 dogs to three diets and records whether each dog's coat improves, stays the same or gets worse. Which test fits?
options: Homogeneity: compare the three diet groups' outcome distributions
A one-proportion z test for the share of dogs that improve
A chi-square test for independence, since the dogs form one group
A two-sample z test, since there are two variables

items.q: In a two-way table, one expected count is 3.2 and the rest are above 8. What does this mean for a chi-square test?
options: Large counts fails, so the p-value from the test may not be accurate
The 3.2 should be rounded to 3 before testing
The test is fine, as long as the observed count in that cell is above 5
The test is fine, because most of the expected counts are large

items.q: A student writes this alternative hypothesis for a test of independence: "<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_a</annotation></semantics></math>: there is an association, and people who exercise sleep more." What is wrong?
options: A chi-square alternative only claims an association, with no direction
It should say there is no association between the variables
It should be written about the sample counts in the table
Exercise is not a categorical variable, so the test does not apply

items.q: A random sample of 200 workers is classified by whether they work from home (80 do, 120 do not) and whether they own a pet. Of those who work from home, 34 own a pet; of the others, 38 do. If working from home and pet ownership are independent, what is the expected count of workers who work from home and own a pet?

mistakes.why: That is the observed count. Expected <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext>row total</mtext><mo>×</mo><mtext>column total</mtext></mrow><mtext>grand total</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{\text{grand total}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
That divides 200 equally over four cells. Use the totals: 80 work from home and 72 own a pet.

items.q: Which study calls for a chi-square test for independence rather than homogeneity?
options: Patients randomly assigned to three treatments, with the outcome recorded as better, same or worse
One random sample of 500 voters, each classified by party and by view on a ballot measure
Random samples of 100 students at four schools, asked their favorite subject
Separate random samples of 200 voters from each of three parties, asked their view on a measure

items.q: What is the value of the chi-square statistic? Give two decimal places.

mistakes.why: That adds the squared gaps <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(O - E)^2</annotation></semantics></math> without dividing each by its expected count <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math>.

The gaps must be squared: each term is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mi>E</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{(O - E)^2}{E}</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: How many degrees of freedom does the test have?

mistakes.why: That is the number of cells minus 1. For a two-way table, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>df</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{df}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>rows</mtext><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>columns</mtext><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= (\text{rows} - 1)(\text{columns} - 1)</annotation></semantics></math>.

That is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n - 1</annotation></semantics></math>. For chi-square, df depends on the table's size: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2 - 1)(3 - 1) = 2</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: What is the p-value? Give four decimal places.

mistakes.why: That uses 5 degrees of freedom. The table has 2 rows and 3 columns, so <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>df</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{df} = 2</annotation></semantics></math>.

That is the area to the left. A chi-square p-value is the area to the right of <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>χ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^2</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: State the conclusion of the test in context.

options: There is convincing evidence of an association between
There is not convincing evidence of an association between
It is proven that there is an association between

why.1: The p-value, 0.0165, is less than 0.05, so the evidence is convincing.
why.2: A test gives evidence; it never proves.

options: keeping a phone in the bedroom and usual sleep, for students at the school
keeping a phone in the bedroom and usual sleep, for the 300 students sampled
phones in the bedroom and less sleep, because phones keep students awake

why.1: The conclusion is about the school's students, the population, not just the sample.
why.2: This is an observational study, so it cannot show that phones cause less sleep.

options: Because 0.0165 < 0.05, reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.0165 > 0.05, fail to reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.0165 > 0.05, reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.0165 < 0.05, accept the null hypothesis.

why.1: Check the inequality: the p-value 0.0165 is less than alpha 0.05, so reject the null hypothesis.
why.2: Reject only when the p-value is less than alpha.
why.3: A test never accepts the null hypothesis; it can only fail to reject it.

conclude.model: Because the p-value of 0.0165 is less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. There is convincing evidence of an association between keeping a phone in the bedroom and usual hours of sleep for students at the school.

items.q: Which cell contributes most to the chi-square statistic, and what does it show?
options: No phone, under 7 hours: 20 observed, 30 expected
Phone, 7 to 8 hours: the largest observed count in the table, 90
Phone, under 7 hours: 70 observed against 60 expected
No phone, over 8 hours: 30 observed against 23.3 expected

items.q: How many degrees of freedom does this test have?

mistakes.why: That is the number of cells minus 1. Use <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2 - 1)(4 - 1)</annotation></semantics></math>.

That is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n - 1</annotation></semantics></math>. Chi-square degrees of freedom come from the table: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>rows</mtext><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>columns</mtext><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\text{rows} - 1)(\text{columns} - 1)</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: What is the p-value for <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>χ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>4.178</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^2 = 4.178</annotation></semantics></math>? Give three decimal places.

mistakes.why: That uses 7 degrees of freedom (cells minus 1). With 2 rows and 4 columns, df = 3.
That uses 1 degree of freedom. With 2 rows and 4 columns, df = 3.

items.q: State the conclusion in context.

options: There is not convincing evidence that
There is convincing evidence that
It is shown that it is false that

why.2: Failing to reject never shows a claim is false; the evidence is just not strong enough.

options: the distribution of results differs between yoga and physical therapy for adults like these
the results of the 200 patients in the study differ between treatments
yoga and physical therapy give the same distribution of results

why.1: The conclusion is about the treatments' effects for patients like these, not just these patients' outcomes.
why.2: That is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math>. A conclusion speaks about <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_a</annotation></semantics></math> and never accepts <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math>.

options: Because 0.243 > 0.05, fail to reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.243 < 0.05, reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.243 > 0.05, reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.243 < 0.05, accept the null hypothesis.

why.1: Check the inequality: the p-value 0.243 is greater than alpha 0.05, so fail to reject the null hypothesis.
why.2: Reject only when the p-value is less than alpha.
why.3: A test never accepts the null hypothesis; it can only fail to reject it.

conclude.model: Because the p-value of 0.243 is greater than 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis. There is not convincing evidence that the distribution of results differs between yoga and physical therapy for adults with lower back pain like these.

items.q: A blog post says, "The clinic's study shows yoga and physical therapy work equally well." What is the best response?
options: The post is right, because the treatments were randomly assigned
The post is right, since the p-value is greater than 0.05
No convincing difference was found; that does not show they are equal
The post is wrong, because yoga had more patients much better, 34 against 22

items.q: Which describes a chi-square distribution?
options: It is symmetric and centered at 0, like the standard normal distribution
It is skewed left, with a long tail toward 0
It has the same shape for each number of degrees of freedom
Values of 0 or more, skewed right, shape set by the df

items.q: In one cell of a two-way table, the observed count is 30 and the expected count is 22.4. Write the expression for this cell's contribution to <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>χ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^2</annotation></semantics></math>, then give its value to two decimal places.

mistakes.why: Divide by the expected count, 22.4, not the observed count.

Square the gap first: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(O - E)^2</annotation></semantics></math>, then divide by <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Two chi-square tests on tables of the same size give <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>χ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>3.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^2 = 3.1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>χ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>14.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^2 = 14.8</annotation></semantics></math>. Which statement is true?
options: The p-values say nothing, because <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>χ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^2</annotation></semantics></math> values are not comparable

The test with <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>χ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>3.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^2 = 3.1</annotation></semantics></math> has the smaller p-value

The test with <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>χ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>14.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^2 = 14.8</annotation></semantics></math> has the smaller p-value
Both tests have the same p-value, since the tables are the same size

items.q: A two-way table classifies students by class year (4 categories) and favorite lunch option (5 categories). How many degrees of freedom does a chi-square test for independence have?

A chi-square test for independence rejects <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math>. Which follow-up best describes the association?

items.q: In the phone and sleep study, what would a Type I error be?
